mcqs.learning_point: Relate first law to balanced forces
mcqs.question: Which of the following comparisons correctly relates Newton’s first law of motion to the condition of balanced forces acting on an object?

options.A: An object at rest remains at rest only when unbalanced forces act on it.
options.B: An object moving with constant speed in a straight line will continue to do so only if the net external force is zero.
options.C: An object will accelerate if the forces are balanced.
options.D: Balanced forces cause a change in the direction of motion.

mcqs.answer: An object moving with constant speed in a straight line will continue to do so only if the net external force is zero.
mcqs.explanation: Newton’s first law (the law of inertia) states that an object will maintain its state of rest or uniform straight‑line motion when the net external force acting on it is zero, i.e., when the forces are balanced. Option B captures this relationship; the other options misinterpret the effect of balanced forces.

mcqs.question: In a competitive‑exam style question, which scenario best illustrates the concept of inertia as described by Newton’s first law?

options.A: A ball rolls down an inclined plane and speeds up because of gravity.
options.B: A passenger lurches forward when a car suddenly stops.
options.C: A kite rises when the wind blows.

mcqs.answer: A passenger lurches forward when a car suddenly stops.
mcqs.explanation: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion. When the car stops abruptly, the passenger’s body tends to continue moving forward, demonstrating inertia. Options A, C, and D involve forces that cause motion rather than resistance to change.

mcqs.question: Newton’s first law of motion is best stated as:

options.A: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
options.B: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass.
options.C: An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion continues in uniform straight‑line motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
options.D: The force acting on an object equals its mass times its velocity.

mcqs.answer: An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion continues in uniform straight‑line motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
mcqs.explanation: Option C is the precise statement of Newton’s first law (the law of inertia). Option A describes the third law, Option B the second law, and Option D is incorrect (force equals mass times acceleration, not velocity).

mcqs.learning_point: Relate first law to balanced forces
mcqs.question: According to Newton’s first law, what will happen to a book lying on a table if the forces acting on it are balanced?
mcqs.explanation: When the net external force on an object is zero (forces are balanced), Newton’s first law tells us the object will maintain its current state. Since the book is initially at rest, it stays at rest. The other options describe motion that requires an unbalanced force.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of inertia?

options.A: A soccer ball remaining stationary until it is kicked.
options.B: A passenger sliding forward when a bus suddenly stops.
options.C: A book sliding faster down a slope because of gravity.
options.D: A cup staying on a moving train’s tray until the train stops.

mcqs.answer: A book sliding faster down a slope because of gravity.
mcqs.explanation: Inertia refers to the resistance to change in motion. Options A, B, and D illustrate objects resisting motion change until an external force acts. Option C describes acceleration due to a net force (gravity) and therefore is not an example of inertia.

mcqs.question: A cyclist rides at a constant speed on a straight, level road and then coasts without pedaling. According to Newton’s first law, why does the cyclist continue moving forward?

options.A: Because the cyclist’s muscles are still providing force.
options.B: Because there is no net external force acting on the cyclist and bike (ignoring friction).
options.C: Because gravity pulls the cyclist forward.
options.D: Because the wheels generate forward thrust automatically.

mcqs.answer: Because there is no net external force acting on the cyclist and bike (ignoring friction).
mcqs.explanation: Newton’s first law states that an object in motion will stay in motion with constant velocity if the net external force is zero. When the cyclist stops pedaling and friction is negligible, the net force is essentially zero, so the motion continues. Options A, C, and D incorrectly attribute continued motion to active forces.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate first law to balanced forces
mcqs.question: Which example best demonstrates the relationship between Newton’s first law and balanced forces?

options.A: A skydiver reaching terminal velocity when air resistance equals his weight.
options.B: A ball being thrown upward and slowing down.
options.C: A car accelerating when the driver presses the accelerator pedal.
options.D: A pendulum swinging back and forth.

mcqs.answer: A skydiver reaching terminal velocity when air resistance equals his weight.
mcqs.explanation: At terminal velocity, the downward gravitational force and the upward air‑resistance force are equal, giving a net force of zero. According to Newton’s first law, the skydiver then moves with constant velocity. Options B, C, and D involve unbalanced forces causing acceleration.

mcqs.question: A tablecloth is quickly pulled from under a set of dishes, and the dishes remain almost stationary. Which principle of inertia explains this observation?

options.A: Objects at rest tend to stay at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
options.B: Objects in motion tend to stay in motion in a circular path.
options.C: Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite.
options.D: The mass of the dishes determines their speed.

mcqs.answer: Objects at rest tend to stay at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
mcqs.explanation: The dishes are initially at rest. The rapid pull on the cloth applies a very brief, small horizontal force, insufficient to overcome the dishes’ inertia, so they remain essentially at rest. This illustrates the first part of Newton’s first law. Options B, C, and D describe unrelated principles.
